stem: Meera points a waterproof torch up from inside a fish tank. The beam hits the water surface at 30° to the normal (water n = 4/3). What does the beam do at the surface?

options.A: It comes out into the air bending toward the normal
options.B: It comes out into the air bending away from the normal
options.C: It is totally reflected back into the water
options.D: It comes out into the air without bending at all

r1.text: Light always bends toward the normal when it goes into a new medium.

r2.text: Water to air means going into a rarer medium, so it bends away, and 30° is less than the critical angle so it still gets out.

r3.text: Light hitting a water surface from below just reflects back fully, the angle doesn't really matter.

stem: Inside Rohan's glass paperweight (n = 1.5), a laser beam reaches the flat top face at 25° to the normal. What happens as the beam passes out into the room air?

options.A: It is totally reflected back into the paperweight
options.B: It bends toward the normal, leaving at less than 25°
options.C: It bends away from the normal, leaving at more than 25°
options.D: It goes straight out because glass and air are both transparent

r1.text: Any time light crosses glass, it bends toward the normal, that's the rule.

r2.text: Light inside glass can always get trapped by total reflection at the surface.

r3.text: Glass to air is dense to rare, so it bends away, and 25° is below 41.8° so it comes out.

stem: A lamp fixed at the bottom of a hotel swimming pool sends a ray up to the water surface at 40° to the normal (water n = 4/3). What happens to this ray?

options.A: It enters the air at about 28.8° from the normal
options.B: It is totally reflected back into the pool
options.C: It enters the air at about 53.3° from the normal
options.D: It enters the air at about 59.0° from the normal

r1.text: Water to air it bends away, so n sin 40° gives sin r = 0.857, about 59°, and 40° is under the critical angle.

r2.text: Underwater light hitting the top just bounces back fully, the pool surface acts like a mirror.

r3.text: It should bend toward the normal, so the angle in air must come out smaller than 40°.

verify_flags: A uses sin r = (3/4) sin 40° = 0.482 -> 28.8° (bending toward normal); C is the slip of multiplying the angle, 40° × 4/3 ≈ 53.3°; 40° < C ≈ 48.6° so no TIR

stem: At a science fair, Kavya shines a laser from air onto a glass block (n = 1.5) at 60° to the normal, which is more than glass's critical angle of 41.8°. What happens at the surface?

options.A: The beam enters the glass, bending toward the normal to about 35°
options.B: Total internal reflection, because 60° is bigger than 41.8°
options.C: The beam enters the glass without bending at all
options.D: All the light reflects back into the air, as the glass acts like a mirror at large angles

r1.text: Once the angle crosses the critical angle, total internal reflection happens, whichever side the light comes from.

r2.text: Total reflection needs light going from glass to air; here it is air to glass, so it just refracts in and bends toward the normal.

r3.text: Light bends toward the normal at every surface, so it goes in bent toward the normal.

verify_flags: Some light is always partially reflected at the surface; option D says ALL light reflects, which is the wrong part. r3 (R3) reaches the right answer for the wrong reason, by design

stem: Light travels inside a glass block (n = 1.5) and then passes out into air at an angle. What is its speed in the glass (c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s), and does it bend toward or away from the normal on leaving? Why?
answer_key: Its speed in glass is 2.0 × 10⁸ m/s, and it bends away from the normal on leaving.
expected_reasoning: v = c/n = 3.0 × 10⁸ / 1.5 = 2.0 × 10⁸ m/s. Going from glass into air it moves into a rarer medium and speeds up, so it bends away from the normal.

slips.why: multiplied by n instead of dividing
assumed light keeps the vacuum speed inside glass

follow_ups.R3: On leaving the glass, light goes from 2.0 × 10⁸ m/s back up to 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s. Is the angle in air bigger or smaller than the angle inside the glass?
follow_ups.CORRECT_NO_REASON: Why does leaving the glass make the ray bend away from the normal and not toward it?
follow_ups.CORRECT: Light of wavelength 600 nm in air enters this glass. What are its frequency and its wavelength inside the glass?
follow_ups.UNCLEAR: Can you give the speed in the glass with its unit, and say in one word whether it bends toward or away from the normal?

verify_flags: CORRECT follow-up answer: f = c/λ = 3.0 × 10⁸ / 600 × 10⁻⁹ = 5.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz (unchanged); λ_glass = 600/1.5 = 400 nm

stem: Sameer says: 'Shine a torch from the air onto a pond at 80° to the normal and the light will be totally internally reflected, because 80° is beyond water's critical angle.' Is he right? Give a reason.
answer_key: No; light going from air into water always refracts into the water, so TIR cannot happen.
expected_reasoning: Total internal reflection needs light travelling from a denser to a rarer medium. From air into water, sin r = sin 80°/(4/3) ≈ 0.74 is less than 1, so a refracted ray always exists.

follow_ups.R4: Before light can be trapped by total internal reflection, which side of the surface must it start on: the air side or the water side?
follow_ups.CORRECT_NO_REASON: Why can a ray coming from the air never be totally internally reflected at a water surface?
follow_ups.CORRECT: An optical fibre carries light around a gentle bend. Which two conditions keep the light trapped inside the glass core?
follow_ups.UNCLEAR: Does the torch light go into the pond, or is all of it reflected? Say which, and why.

verify_flags: Water n = 4/3 assumed; some light is partially reflected at any surface, which is not TIR

stem: A diver's torch underwater sends a ray up to the water surface at 60° to the normal (water n = 4/3, critical angle ≈ 48.6°). What happens to the ray at the surface, and why?
answer_key: It is totally internally reflected back into the water.
expected_reasoning: The ray goes from denser water toward rarer air, and 60° is greater than the critical angle of about 48.6°, so no refracted ray exists and all the light reflects back.

follow_ups.R3: Is the ray going from denser to rarer or rarer to denser here, and which way does that make it bend if it does get out?
follow_ups.CORRECT_NO_REASON: Which two conditions did you check to decide the ray stays trapped in the water?
follow_ups.CORRECT: Diamond has n ≈ 2.42, so its critical angle is only about 24°. Why does that help a cut diamond sparkle more than glass?
follow_ups.UNCLEAR: Does any of this ray leave the water into the air? Yes or no, and why?

calc: sin C = 3/4 = 0.75 -> C ≈ 48.6°; (4/3) × sin 60° = 1.155 > 1, so no refracted ray

stem: A ray of light in air strikes the flat surface of a glass block (n = 1.5). The ray makes an angle of 60° with the glass surface. What is the angle of refraction inside the glass?

options.D: The ray is totally internally reflected at the surface

r1.text: The angle of incidence is measured from the normal, so it is 90° − 60° = 30°; then sin r = sin 30° / 1.5.

r2.text: The angle of incidence is the angle between the ray and the glass surface, so I put 60° into Snell's law.

r3.text: At such a slanting angle the light can't get in, so it all reflects back.

steps.text: Angle of incidence from the normal: i = 90° − 60° = 30°.
steps.trap_text: using the 60° to the surface as the angle of incidence.

steps.text: Snell's law, air into glass: sin r = sin 30° ÷ 1.5 = 0.333.
steps.trap_text: expecting total internal reflection; it can't happen going from air into denser glass.
giving the angle from the surface (90° − r) instead of from the normal.

stem: A laser beam inside water (n = 4/3) meets the water surface, making an angle of 50° with the surface. At what angle to the normal does it come out into the air? Show which angle you used.
expected_reasoning: The ray makes 50° with the surface, so the angle of incidence from the normal is 40°. Then sin r = (4/3) sin 40° = 0.857, so r is about 59.0°.

slips.why: divide by 4/3 instead of multiplying (sin r = sin 40° ÷ 4/3)

follow_ups.R7: Draw the normal where the beam meets the surface. What angle does the beam make with that line?
follow_ups.R3: Is the light going into a denser or a rarer medium here? Which way should it bend?
follow_ups.CORRECT_NO_REASON: Which angle did you put into Snell's law, and which line did you measure it from?
follow_ups.CORRECT: At what angle to the surface would this beam just begin to be totally internally reflected?
follow_ups.UNCLEAR: Which angle did you use in Snell's law, and which line did you measure it from?

steps.text: Angle of incidence from the normal: i = 90° − 50° = 40°.
steps.trap_text: using the 50° to the surface as the angle of incidence.

steps.text: Snell's law, water into air: (4/3) × sin 40° = sin r, so sin r = 1.333 × 0.643 = 0.857.
steps.trap_text: dividing by 4/3 instead of multiplying, which gives r ≈ 28.8°.

steps.text: r = sin⁻¹(0.857) ≈ 59° from the normal: the ray bends away from the normal.
steps.trap_text: giving the angle from the surface (31°) instead of from the normal.
